segments.say: We're nearly at the end of our evening together. If you're still listening, that's lovely. And if you've already drifted off, that's lovely too. These last few words are just a soft blanket of sound, something to rest under while the night grows deeper and quieter around you.

Somewhere in our story, Nora has fallen asleep too. Her big window is dark now, the curtains half open. Outside, the sea keeps its slow rhythm, waves arriving and leaving on the sand below. She doesn't need to watch it. It will carry on all night without her, faithful and patient and calm.

Her first year in that little flat taught her something gentle. The big thrill of the view didn't last. It was never going to. But in its place, something quieter grew. A small pause at the window in the morning. Three good things at night. A friend's delighted face, reminding her what she had stopped seeing. Not fireworks. Something warmer, and steadier, and kinder.

If tonight had one thread running through it, maybe it was this. Good things fade. That's how the brain is built, and it isn't a flaw. Fading is not failing. We can look again, and slow down, and share good moments with other people. And the small things, the ordinary, quiet things, have a way of returning, again and again, if we let them.

Your brain has worked hard today. Noticing, comparing, predicting, getting used to things so you can pay attention to what's new. It's a loyal helper, even when it lets the shine wear off. Tonight, it can rest from all of that. Nothing needs predicting. Nothing needs comparing. It can simply drift, the way the sea drifts under the moon.

And tomorrow, when you wake, some ordinary thing might catch your eye in a new way. Light on a wall. The smell of morning air. A familiar face. You don't need to plan for it, or try to make it happen. Just know that it's possible. The world has a way of looking new again, when we give it a gentle second glance.

Picture the window again, but in the morning. Pale gold light spreading across the water. A curtain moving gently in the breeze. The same sea as last night, the same sea as the first day, and yet somehow new. It waited all night, without any fuss, ready to be seen as if for the very first time.

show.cap: The sea will still be there

segments.say: Do you remember the evening Nora's friend came to visit? She stepped into the little flat, saw the window, and simply stopped, with her hand over her mouth. And in that moment, Nora saw the sea again too, through someone else's eyes. Good things often come back to us that way. Through the people we share them with, and the small, surprised joy on a familiar face.

Even now, as you lie here, there may be people somewhere near you. Sleeping in another room, or in another house down the street, or far away in another town. People you love, people you've met only once, people you'll never meet at all. All of them resting under the same dark sky tonight, breathing slowly, letting the day go, just like you.

And if, on some ordinary day, the shine seems to have worn off everything, there are small ways back. A pause at a window. Three good things at the end of a day. A moment shared with someone else. A gentle second glance at something you've stopped seeing. None of them is magic. But each one is a small door, and small doors are easy to open.

For now, there's nothing to hold on to and nothing to chase. Not happiness, not sleep, not even these words. Happiness, as we heard tonight, often comes most easily when we stop running after it. Sleep is just the same. Let it come in its own time, like a wave rolling slowly toward the shore.

Notice your breath one last time. In, gently. Out, a little longer. A small pause. It has been with you all evening, all day, all your life, quietly carrying on. It will carry on all night too, while you rest. You don't need to watch over it. It knows exactly what to do.

Here is one last thought to carry into sleep. Let it come, let it go. Joy and worry, light and dark, waves on the shore. Everything arrives, and everything leaves, and underneath it all, something calm and deep stays just as it is. You can rest in that calm now. It has been there all along.

show.text: Let it come, let it go.

segments.say: If you can, offer yourself one small kindness before you sleep. Not a task. Just a warm thought, the kind you'd give a friend at the end of a long day. You did well today. You can rest now. You don't need to be any happier than you are, right here, right now, warm and safe and still.

Thank you for spending this evening with me. For following Nora through her first year by the sea, for meeting the twins and the students and the travellers on their trains, and for taking this slow walk at the end of it all. Whatever your own days bring, I hope you can meet the good parts with fresh eyes, now and then.

Sleep well. Let the waves keep their slow time. Let the breath stay soft and easy. Let the night hold you, the way it has held people for as long as there have been people, and evenings, and quiet rooms with the sound of the sea outside.

So rest now. A warm bed beneath you. A slow breath inside you. A quiet sea, somewhere in your mind, rolling gently onto the sand. And a long, gentle night ahead, with nothing to do and nowhere to be. Everything is just as it should be. You can let go.

Let yourself drift now, further and further, out with the tide. The sound of this voice growing softer and softer, like waves heard from far away. The room growing darker and warmer. The breath growing slower and deeper. Further, and further, and further still, until there's only rest.

The night ahead is long and calm. There's plenty of time. Time to rest, time to dream, time to simply be still. And in the morning, the world will be waiting, ordinary and familiar, and, if you look at it gently, just a little bit new. Goodnight, for now. Rest easy.

Next time, we'll explore a very different feeling, one that rises fast and burns hot. Why do we get angry, what is anger really for, and what is happening in the brain when it flares? We'll look at all of it gently, in Why We Get Angry. But that's for another night. For now, rest easy. Goodnight.
